subject: Re: Concurrency & rate limits — post-call notes and next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Michael Stone <michael.stone@acme.com>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 24 Aug 2026 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call recap: concurrency & streaming requirements

Hi Michael / Natalie —

Thanks again for the call today. Quick recap of what I took away and a proposed set of next steps so we can align engineering and procurement: 

Summary of regen requirements (please confirm):
- Primary use: user-facing chat + async batch scoring for personalization.
- Typical sustained concurrency: ~150 concurrent requests during business hours.
- Burst concurrency: up to ~650 concurrent requests (30–45 minutes, once per day).
- Connection pattern: ~50 frontend instances with connection pooling; each instance may open up to 10 simultaneous HTTP connections to Redwood (so ~500 simultaneous connections at peak).
- Streaming: chat uses streaming for token-by-token updates (~15–20 tokens/s per session); low tolerance for tail latency.
- Latency targets: 95th percentile generation latency goal <= 300ms for short responses (<=128 tokens); streaming token latency goal <= 200ms tail.

Open asks / items for Redwood to confirm:
1) Can we support the peak concurrency and connection counts without significant throttling on the hosted plan, or should Acme move to Dedicated/reserved capacity?
2) Proposed soft/hard concurrency limits and per-minute token caps for your account tier.
3) Any special config recommendations for connection pooling and keep-alive to reduce head-of-line impacts.
4) Proposed timeline for a two-week canary + metrics we should instrument.

Next steps I propose:
- Dev session: schedule a 45-minute technical call with Dev and Rishi this week to walk through traffic profile and connection pooling (Dev to propose times).
- I’m attaching an SLO matrix and Redwood rate limits PDF so you can see standard defaults.
- I’ll follow up with a mutual action plan and a preliminary proposal for increasing concurrency quotas if needed.

Attachments: SLO_matrix_v2.xlsx (spreadsheet), redwood-rate-limits.pdf (doc)

Thanks — talk soon.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Enterprise Account Executive
Redwood Inference

From: Michael Stone <michael.stone@acme.com>

Cc: Natalie Gomez <natalie.gomez@acme.com>, Acme Platform Team <platform@acme.com>
Date: Tue, 25 Aug 2026 09:08:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call recap: concurrency & streaming requirements

Marissa —

Thanks for the clear summary. Confirming the numbers are in the right ballpark. A few clarifications from our side:
- Sustained concurrency: we generally see 120–180 during business hours, so 150 is a good median.
- Bursts: the 650 number is accurate; these bursts correlate with our nightly personalization batch that fans out requests across the cluster for scoring (lasting ~20–40 minutes).
- Connections: correct — our frontends use a connection pool, roughly 50 instances x up to 10 connections each. We can tune that number if required, but it's important we can support the connection count rather than serializing.
- Streaming: chat sessions are interactive; some sessions last several minutes. We need streaming tail latency to be stable.

Can you share what Redwood would propose as soft/hard concurrency limits? Also include any per-API-key connection limits (if applicable). Finally, do you have guidance for keep-alive timeout and recommended HTTP client settings for Node/Go?

Appreciate the attachments — I’ll review and circle back after the tech call.

Michael Stone
Head of Platform
Acme Corp
michael.stone@acme.com
From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>
To: Michael Stone <michael.stone@acme.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 25 Aug 2026 11:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call recap: concurrency & streaming requirements

Michael —

Appreciate the detail. A few technical notes from our ops/solutions side so we can size things correctly:

- Connection pooling: best practice is long-lived keep-alive with max 100s idle timeout on our side; client-side keep-alive and HTTP/1.1 persistent connections work fine. For Node we recommend setting agent.keepAlive = true and increasing maxSockets to match desired parallelism; for Go use http.Transport with MaxIdleConnsPerHost tuned.
- We recommend a per-instance connection cap (e.g., 8) to reduce head-of-line blocking; that said, we can support 10–12 if Acme needs it — but we’ll prioritize streaming traffic in our routing when under pressure.
- Streaming prioritization: we can mark streaming connections and bias scheduling to keep tail latency low (this is part of the Dedicated offering; on hosted plans prioritization is limited).
- KV/prefix caching: for repeated prompts (e.g., personalization templates) enabling prefix caching can reduce per-request compute and improve p95.

I’ve attached an updated SLO matrix with examples mapped to your traffic profile.

Attachments: SLO_matrix_v2.xlsx

Happy to discuss on the tech call — I can demo connection pool behavior quickly.

— Dev
Senior Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
To: Michael Stone <michael.stone@acme.com>, Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 26 Aug 2026 08:30:00 -0700
Subject: Proposed concurrency/quota settings for Acme (draft)

Michael / team —

Following our discussion and Dev's notes, here is a draft set of limits we can offer as a starting point. These are intended to be conservative but flexible for a two-week canary: 

- Soft concurrency quota: 800 concurrent API requests (soft limit, throttles with 429s after soft but allows short bursts).
- Hard concurrency cap: 1,000 concurrent API requests (hard limit — connections beyond this will be rejected).
- Per-API-key connection limit: 2,000 simultaneous connections total, with per-worker suggested cap of 12.
- Per-minute token cap: 10,000,000 tokens/minute (to prevent noisy neighbors in multi-tenant; can be scoped per route).
- Streaming prioritization: enable tag for chat route; we will schedule streaming tokens ahead of batch gen tokens under pressure.
- Canary plan: 2-week canary with real traffic, split 20%/80% (Acme/Rest) routing to monitor p95 latency and error rates. Rollback criteria: p95 > 500ms for generation or >2% 5xx rate.

Caveats: per-request latency is influenced by prompt length, model choice, and batch sizing. If Acme needs guaranteed p95 <300ms at peak 1k concurrency for large prompts we will likely recommend Dedicated capacity and an SLO contract, because multi-tenant hosting introduces variability.

If that works, Marissa can put together the mutual action plan and we’ll schedule the engineering session this week.

— Rishi
Staff Engineer, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference
